implementation_notes: CAF is a mature C++ actor framework: an actor_system supplies the scheduler, registry and internal mailbox documented as a concurrent many-writers-single-reader queue; an event-based actor owns its state and only messages modify it, and its behavior may be statically or dynamically typed. Event-based actors are scheduled cooperatively and cost a few hundred bytes each, while a potentially starving actor can be detached to run on its own thread. Links and monitors supply failure propagation, so supervision does not have to be invented. Choose CAF when you want a runtime with remoting, supervision or streaming; for a handful of actors the hand-rolled variant is smaller and dependency-free.
pitfalls: Event-based actors are cooperatively scheduled: a blocking call inside a handler starves other actors; detach the actor or move blocking work to a dedicated thread.
A handler must touch state only through the message loop; capturing external mutable state by reference in a behavior recreates the shared-memory race the pattern avoids.
Mailboxes are unbounded by default, so bursty load grows memory unless a size limit and full policy are configured.

variants.name: Hand-rolled std::thread + condition-variable mailbox
variants.implementation_notes: The standard library gives the pieces but no mailbox: a class owns its state plus a std::queue<Msg> guarded by a std::mutex and a std::condition_variable, and one std::thread runs the receive loop using the predicated cv.wait overload. Shutdown is a sentinel message or a done flag followed by notify_all, and messages should be move-only values so the sender demonstrably gives up ownership, as Rust enforces. Choose this when a dependency on an actor runtime is unacceptable or the actors are few; the classic structure is justified precisely because C++ offers no mailbox.
pitfalls: The predicated cv.wait against queue emptiness is mandatory: a bare wait wakes on spurious wakeups and on unrelated notifications.
Messages must be moved, not copied, when the actor takes ownership; a shared_ptr payload quietly reintroduces shared mutable state.
A thread per actor does not scale past a few dozen actors; multiplex many actors over a thread pool or an event loop.
